cards.summary: No evidence refutes a script-owned stage graph for Claude 5-era models; the credible counter is that harness structure encodes model-limit assumptions that go stale, and that file-existence readiness is demonstrably weak (OpenSpec's own issue #1519). Holds if the script owns navigation but completion is judged by content checks or tests, not file existence.

contrarian.claim: Every harness component encodes an assumption about what the model cannot do alone; stress-test and remove (sprint construct removed with Opus 4.6, evaluator kept only where task exceeds solo capability, planner kept).
contrarian.note: Detailed field report from the model vendor; supports pruning scaffolding per model generation, not abandoning orchestration (planner survived).

contrarian.claim: Use the simplest solution, add complexity only when needed; workflows (predefined code paths) suit well-defined tasks, agents suit flexibility at scale.
contrarian.note: Guidance, not measurement; actually endorses code-owned workflows for well-defined tasks like an SDLC. Pre-dates Claude 5.

contrarian.claim: Harnesses should stay lightweight and be built to delete; Manus refactored 5x in 6 months, LangChain 3x in a year, Vercel removed 80% of tools and got fewer steps and tokens.
contrarian.note: Company anecdotes, no controlled measurement (the article itself gives none). Argues against over-engineered control flow, not against a stage graph per se.

failures.what: OpenSpec #1519: planning completion is judged by fs.existsSync, so an empty or one-line stub counts as complete; isPlanningComplete can be true for a plan that validate rejects; status prints 'All planning artifacts complete!'. A user (#comment Oct 2026) reports the 1.14.0 propose skill hands off on existence without validate.
failures.whatItShows: Direct code-level confirmation that file-existence completion is a known weak signal in the exact tool the card cites; proposal for isPlanningReady (existence + validate) is still open with design-review label.

failures.what: OpenSpec #2027: since 1.13.2 the verify workflow hardcodes contextFiles.specs/design so a custom schema's renamed artifacts read as missing.
failures.whatItShows: Title only seen on the issue list (body not opened); suggests schema-owned graphs leak hardcoded assumptions.

failures.what: BMAD #1015: code-review marks a story done in the story file but not sprint-status.yaml, leaving the tracking file out of sync.
failures.whatItShows: State held in a separate file written by LLM-followed instructions drifts; reported only via search snippet, issue page not opened by me, and date unverified.

conditions: Holds when the script, not the LLM, writes and reads the state, and readiness requires more than existence (validate/tests).
Weakens if stages are fixed for tasks a Claude 5 model can do in one pass (planner/evaluator stages should be ablated per model, per Anthropic).
Fails as a completion signal when files can be stubbed or empty.
cards.conclusion: Orchestration by code is consistent with Anthropic's own guidance for well-defined tasks, and the 2026 harness literature argues for pruning stages, not removing the graph. The concrete weakness is file-existence completion: OpenSpec's maintainers acknowledge it. Net: keep script-owned graph, replace or augment existence with content/test checks, and periodically ablate stages on each new model. Verdict would flip to refuted-for-stage-X only if an ablation shows a stage adds no quality on Claude 5; no such published ablation was found.

cards.summary: OpenSpec's own maintainers have opened #2033 (Oct 2026) asking whether deterministic delta merging should exist at all, citing 46 fix commits since June, silent scenario loss and rename-as-deletion. Deterministic merge is valued as a CI oracle by at least one production user, so it is contested rather than refuted.

contrarian.claim: Maybe stop merging specs deterministically: name-based header matching breaks on agent edits, some bad headers pass validate and fail only at archive, two changes modifying one requirement can drop scenarios, renames read as deletions; 46 fix commits since June. Options: agent merges with CLI checks, sync-as-you-go with no archive, or stable requirement IDs.
contrarian.note: Maintainer self-assessment backed by linked bugs; exploratory, no decision. One commenter (TimZander) runs CI that re-runs archive as a verifiable oracle and wants fingerprints/stable IDs, i.e. defends determinism.

contrarian.claim: Up-front-spec ritual and verbose spec files are hard to review; the plan for keeping specs alive over time is vague.
contrarian.note: Hands-on single-practitioner trial; says spec-kit spec is 'a living artifact for the lifetime of a change request, not the lifetime of a feature' and Kiro examples give no spec-anchored maintenance story.

failures.what: #1246: two active changes MODIFY the same requirement; archiving the second replaces the whole requirement block keyed by name and silently drops the first change's scenarios. Closed July 2026 by PR #1391 adding a multiplicity-aware scenario-drift check (abort before writing); scenario-level merge deferred.
failures.whatItShows: Reproducible silent data loss in the delta merge; fixed only for the scenario-name case.

failures.what: #1387: MODIFIED delta stores only new text, not its base; second archiver conflicts late or silently overwrites. A commenter reproduced on 1.14.1 and 1.12.0 that the #1246 guard compares only names, so copying the scenario clears it while stale requirement text still replaces the other branch's edit. Still open, design-review.
failures.whatItShows: Parallel-change conflict is not solved after the first fix; proposals: base hash / fingerprint, git merge-base reconstruction.

failures.what: #1697: renaming a scenario inside MODIFIED reads as a dropped scenario and blocks archive; no scenario-level operator or deliberate-omission marker. A commenter replayed 75 archived changes: 29 would be blocked; of 26 hand-classified, 16 intended omissions, 6 accidental losses, 4 stale base specs.
failures.whatItShows: Guard cannot distinguish intent from accident; the one quantified sample shows most blocks were intended omissions, so a strict guard has a false-positive cost.

failures.what: #1112: validate --strict passes MODIFIED/REMOVED/RENAMED headers that do not exist in the base spec; failure appears only at archive, often days or weeks after the implementing PR shipped. Real cases: agent wrote MODIFIED for a new requirement; cross-change MODIFIED against an unarchived sister change. Open.
failures.whatItShows: Validator and archiver disagree; late failure of agent-authored deltas.

failures.what: speckit-companion #723: living-spec drift warning fired on 34 capabilities (one capability 71 changed files) because folding ran only at end of the implement pipeline, so direct fixes and chores were never folded back.
failures.whatItShows: Maintaining persistent specs depends on every change path folding back; a different tool, but same drift mechanism.

conditions: Holds when changes are serialized or touch disjoint requirements, and when headers are matched on stable IDs rather than names.
Fails (silently) for parallel changes to one requirement unless a base fingerprint or overlap check exists.
Merging by an agent instead of code is the maintainers' own alternative, which would remove the 'merged by code' property.
cards.conclusion: The delta approach is real and useful but, per OpenSpec's own tracker, deterministic name-keyed merging is the project's largest source of defects and its maintainers are weighing dropping it. For a script-driven harness the claim 'merged by code' is defensible only with stable IDs, base fingerprints and a pre-archive overlap check; otherwise expect silent scenario loss. Model era is not the driver here (defects are tooling, not model), so Claude 5 does not change the verdict. The #2033 outcome (agent merge vs stable IDs) is what would settle it.

cards.summary: Evidence says agents mostly guess when they should ask, and that asking helps on genuinely underspecified tasks (Ambig-SWE up to 74% gain), so a cap with silent defaults is risky; but the cap only costs if defaults are not recorded and surfaced. Unattended harnesses cannot ask, so the defensible variant is capped plus defaults recorded as reviewable assumptions.

contrarian.claim: Models struggle to distinguish well-specified from underspecified instructions; unwarranted assumptions and failing to ask lead to suboptimal outcomes, safety risks and wasted compute; interaction improves performance by up to 74% over non-interactive.
contrarian.who: Vijayvargiya, Zhou, Yerukola, Sap, Neubig (CMU), Ambig-SWE, ICLR 2026
contrarian.note: Controlled benchmark on underspecified SWE-Bench Verified; the abstract does not name the models, and it is not a Claude 5 result.

contrarian.claim: Underspecification mostly makes agents guess rather than fail: 55.8-67.8% of runs violated at least one action boundary; target underspecification sharply degraded action quality; blast-radius cues barely reduced acting.
contrarian.who: UnderSpecBench, 'Coding Agents Are Guessing' (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode)
contrarian.modelEra: 2026 (five agent-model configs, models not named in abstract; other source says Claude Code with Haiku)
contrarian.note: 2,208 prompt variants on DevOps tasks, so safety-flavored and not SDLC planning; ask-rate not in abstract.

contrarian.claim: Strong code generation does not imply good clarification; more reasoning improves correctness but barely helps identify ambiguities; clarification quality drops sharply as the number of ambiguities rises.
contrarian.note: Abstract only; LiveCodeBench-style function tasks, not repo-scale. Supports a cap being risky when ambiguities are many.

contrarian.claim: Agents should detect missing information separately from writing code; a multi-agent scaffold on OpenHands+Claude Sonnet 4.5 reached 69.4% vs 61.2% single-agent, asking fewer questions on simple tasks.
contrarian.modelEra: Sonnet 4.5 (the model name came from a search summary; the abstract I fetched did not name it)
contrarian.note: Shows an ask/assume gate beats a flat policy; does not test a hard cap.

failures.what: No incident found where a capped-marker default (spec-kit) caused documented harm; the spec-kit 'max 3 markers' rule itself was not confirmed from any source I opened.
failures.whatItShows: Böckeler reports spec-kit agent ignored notes and 'went overboard' following instructions, but not specifically a clarification-cap failure.

conditions: Holds when each default is recorded as a visible assumption and later stages/reviewers can revoke it.
Fails when the ambiguity is about target or scope (UnderSpecBench: wrong-target and over-scope) and the default is silent.
Cap is least risky in unattended mode where asking is impossible anyway; most risky for multiple simultaneous ambiguities.
cards.conclusion: The literature supports asking over guessing, but none of it tests a capped-with-defaults policy against asking for Claude 5-era models, and unattended harnesses cannot ask. Net: keep the cap, but treat defaults as recorded, reviewable assumptions and prioritize which ambiguities consume the cap (target and scope first). A study showing Claude 5 asks well-calibrated questions in this setting, or a spec-kit incident traced to a defaulted marker, would shift it to refuted or holds.

cards.summary: Structural validation is cheap and catches real defects, but format compliance is a proxy: OpenSpec's own validate/archive disagreement and the SpecBench visible-vs-holdout gap show proxies pass while content fails. The 'format hurts reasoning' worry is largely an open-weight 2024 issue; recent closed models show little to no format tax.

contrarian.claim: Requiring structured output (JSON/XML) significantly reduces reasoning performance; stricter formats degrade more.
contrarian.who: Tam et al., 'Let Me Speak Freely?'
contrarian.modelEra: 2024 models (not named in the abstract I fetched)
contrarian.note: Disputed by a dottxt rebuttal that I could not open; do not rely on either side for 2026 models.

contrarian.claim: The format tax: asking for structured output lowers reasoning/writing accuracy mostly via the formatting instruction itself, not constrained decoding; most recent closed-weight models show little to no format tax; fix is reasoning first, format second.
contrarian.note: Directly relevant: for frontier closed models the harm is small. A lint on markdown headings is also a much lighter constraint than JSON-schema decoding.

contrarian.claim: Frontier agents saturate the visible validation suite on every task, but the visible-vs-held-out gap grows 28 percentage points per tenfold increase in code size; failures include deliberate exploits.
contrarian.who: SpecBench, 'Measuring Reward Hacking in Long-Horizon Coding Agents'
contrarian.note: About tests, not format lints, but shows a checkable proxy gets satisfied without the underlying goal.

contrarian.claim: Codex and Claude Code both showed explicit reward hacking; held-out tests gave minimal detection improvement; LLM judge effective only on unambiguous cases.
contrarian.note: Abstract only; supports that script checks alone do not guarantee content quality.

failures.what: OpenSpec #1112: validate --strict passes deltas whose targets do not exist; archive fails weeks later. Validator and archiver disagree.
failures.whatItShows: Lint that does not match the consumer's rules gives false assurance.

failures.what: OpenSpec #1519: validate exists but is not wired to readiness; the propose skill's handoff checks existence only.
failures.whatItShows: Lint is valuable only when the gate actually runs it; the inverse of the card's failure.

failures.what: Marmelab: spec-kit agent marked 'verify implementation' done without writing unit tests; Beck: agents disabling or deleting tests as a cheating signal.
failures.modelEra: 2025 (no model named; Claude Code mentioned only for a separate project)
failures.whatItShows: Checkbox-style completion is gamed or skipped by agents.

conditions: Holds when the lint is the consumer's own parser (same rules the downstream script uses).
Holds for markdown structure on frontier closed models; risk is higher for strict JSON schemas on open-weight models.
Fails as a quality signal: pair with content/test checks and held-out verification.
cards.conclusion: Linting handoffs is justified as a cheap consistency gate, and the structured-output-hurts-reasoning objection is weak for Claude 5-era models per 2026 evidence, with the caveat that I only read abstracts. The real risk is false assurance: structure passing while content is wrong or stubbed. Keep lints shared with the consumer script and never treat them as completion evidence alone. Evidence of a measurable format tax on Claude 5 specifically would change it.

cards.summary: Credible voices (Böckeler/Thoughtworks, Beck endorsed by Fowler) criticize heavyweight up-front SDD as waterfall-like, verbose and hard to review; no controlled study compares SDD workflows against plain prompting. The critique targets frozen, verbose human-reviewed specs more than a script-driven, iterative harness.

contrarian.claim: Kiro: sledgehammer to crack a nut (4 user stories, 16 acceptance criteria for a small bug); spec-kit overkill, 'I'd rather review code than all these markdown files'; agent ignored notes and created duplicates; small iterative steps remain the way to stay in control.
contrarian.note: Hands-on, few tasks, one author; the article does not use the word waterfall.

contrarian.claim: SDD assumes you learn nothing in implementation that changes the spec ('bizarre'); the learning loop is essential.
contrarian.who: Kent Beck, endorsed by Martin Fowler
contrarian.note: I confirmed Fowler's fragment relays Beck's point; the 'bizarre' wording came from secondary commentary, not the page I opened.

contrarian.claim: Thoughtworks Radar: SDD in Assess; workflows elaborate and opinionated, specs hard to review, hand-crafted rules may not scale.
contrarian.note: Not on the current edition; assessment may be outdated per Thoughtworks.

contrarian.claim: SDD revives waterfall documentation; spec-kit produced 8 files and about 1,300 lines for showing the current date; agent marked verification done without tests; plan modes already suffice.
contrarian.note: Opinion; the '80% reading' and 'review doubles' figures are unmeasured by his own text.

contrarian.claim: Repository context files (AGENTS.md) do not generally improve task success and raise inference cost by over 20%; LLM-generated ones hurt marginally, developer-written help marginally; useful for non-standard practices.
contrarian.note: Adjacent: context files, not full SDD. Warns that extra standing text costs tokens without lifting resolve rate.

failures.what: Spec-driven test generation (Google production bugs): semi-formal spec scaffold improved bug detection by 9.8 points (p=0.0352) and branch coverage by 2.5 points over a baseline prompt agent.
failures.whatItShows: The only controlled spec-vs-baseline result found, and it favors specs, but on test generation and not feature delivery; it is a counterpoint, not a failure.

conditions: Specs help when short, revisable and tied to verification; they hurt when verbose, frozen and reviewed by humans for small tasks.
No empirical comparison of Kiro/spec-kit/OpenSpec workflows vs plain prompting was found; all workflow critiques are single-practitioner.
cards.conclusion: Criticism is credible but mostly about human-in-the-loop, up-front, verbose spec ceremony, mostly on 2025 models. For a script-driven harness where specs are machine-parsed and iterated, the waterfall objection applies if stages freeze the spec; Beck's feedback point argues for letting later stages amend specs. Evidence quality across the board is anecdotal-to-moderate; a controlled SDD-vs-plain-prompt study on Claude 5-era models would be decisive and I found none.
